title: The Promises and Pitfalls of LLM Annotations in Dataset Labeling: a Case Study on Media Bias Detection

live_model.evidence: two closed-source models GPT-4-turbo and GPT-3.5-turbo, to cover the closed-source state-of-the-art (Section 4.2); Table 4 lists 'openai/gpt-4-turbo'; Table 1 row GPT-4 Turbo

prompt.location: Appendix Table 8 (pseudo-code template with system prompt 'You are an expert in media bias.' and the classification instruction)
prompt.note: The 0-shot + system-prompt variant is fully determined by Table 8; few-shot variants retrieve per-instance examples from BABE.

claim.location: Table 1, row GPT-4 Turbo, column '0-shot + sys prompt' (BABE train/development combined set)

data.source: BABE dataset (Spinde et al. 2021; 4,121 sentences); code at github.com/Media-Bias-Group/annomatic

notes: Alias risk: candidate models come from a late-2023 Open LLM leaderboard snapshot, so the GPT-4 Turbo run may predate the 2024-04-09 GA snapshot; the paper (NAACL Findings 2025) gives no run date or preview string. Exact n of the combined train/dev split must be taken from the BABE release. GPT-4 Turbo was excluded from the final annotator pool for cost.

resolution.plan: n is unprinted because the set is the official BABE train split: the paper uses the authors' 75/25 split with a 1,000-sentence test set, so the train/development combined set is the remaining ~3,121 of 4,121 sentences. Run the Table 8 zero-shot + system prompt ('You are an expert in media bias.') on that split with gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 at temperature 0 and compute MCC vs Table 1 (0.683).
resolution.approximation: Split taken from the BABE release; the paper's 'openai/gpt-4-turbo' alias is resolved to the 2024-04-09 GA snapshot by rule although the run date is not given.
